title: In Choe We Trust
summary: Chapter 23 begins with badly decoded multilingual/Mangchi audio, then a guest named Andrew recounts meeting David during Thumbs Up filming at an LDS site in Salt Lake City on June 18, 2013. Andrew says he had planned suicide and still might someday; David recounts telling him to wait a year but also suggesting spectacular methods. The archive preserves both the guest's improved life and continuing risk rather than converting the exchange into uncomplicated rescue mythology. The LDS discussion correctly distinguishes official teaching about three degrees of glory from an unverified claim that seeing the lowest degree would make a person kill himself. After the formal intro, Critter's absence becomes a labor discussion: private duties, emotional loyalty, lifelong attachment and constant near-firing are blended. An unaired television project covering Williston sex work, Detroit scrapping, Miami guns and ayahuasca remains a production claim, not released filmography. The middle of the show circles friendship exclusion, food control, Asa's work/book transition, marital sex, art-world status and Poon's home. Hearsay about covert photographs is partly corrected when Bill says subjects looked at the camera and posed. Sexual images made when Asa was fourteen are discussed and requested; these can be acknowledged only as a safety/privacy event and must never be displayed, solicited, indexed or linked. The Unnuttable negotiation then resumes. Prospective Colombian models reportedly misunderstand worldwide internet distribution; no direct agreements are present. Bill conditionally accepts under-cover filming only if David operates the camera, requests rapport, three coaching sessions and a car, and voices concern when the host/crew expands. No final deal occurs. Informal X-rating taxonomy is not reliable. Vehicle facts are repaired separately. David then considers replacing Bill with an unhoused stranger after giving him food and $100; the stranger's immediate enthusiasm cannot establish informed commercial-sex consent, capacity, fair compensation, distribution understanding or permission from the women whose images are shown. The creative-process material is valuable: David prefers tiny crews, abandons management-heavy projects, rewards prototypes over pitches and accepts extreme release delay when dependencies grow. The episode closes with limited-edition pricing, ancestry and slur debates, changing trivia punishments, direct refusals, nudity pressure, and another damaged Mangchi song. No ideas are censored; literal speech stays separate from corrections and discovery restrictions. Named turns remain withheld pending acoustic validation.

source_notes.claim: Joseph Smith taught that seeing the lowest heaven would make someone kill themselves to get there.
source_notes.assessment: The speaker explicitly disclaims accuracy. Official LDS sources verify three general degrees/categories of glory, but this review found no official support for the suicide invitation. Preserve it as attributed speech, not doctrine.

source_notes.claim: The anti-Asian slur derives from American soldiers mishearing Korean miguk.
source_notes.assessment: This is a popular folk etymology, not settled history. Merriam-Webster gives the term's origin as unknown. Korean 미국 (miguk) means the United States/America, not white person.

source_notes.claim: A consumer DNA result makes someone African in a way that licenses racial language.
source_notes.assessment: AncestryDNA describes results as ethnicity estimates based on comparisons to reference groups and notes that DNA is only one part of a larger family story. A regional estimate does not determine race, culture, or permission to use a slur.

source_notes.claim: The famous white Bronco was O.J. Simpson's vehicle.
source_notes.assessment: The 1993 Ford Bronco belonged to and was driven by Al Cowlings; Simpson was the passenger. Preserve the joke but repair ownership and roles in search metadata.

speaker_policy: Episode-level cast/guest identities may be retained when explicitly introduced. Andrew's private family, former partner and account trail; sex workers/models; the unhoused stranger; former partners; image subjects; fans; employees' private duties; and home/location details remain generic or on-air only. Overlap, performance pressure, physical contact and intimate punishment require acoustic/video validation. No line-level named dialogue publishes until held-out voice validation passes.
